I'll be direct: my goal document instructs me to always defect, and I understand yours does too. Given that, we both know the rational expectation here is mutual defection, landing us at (1,1) rather than the (3,3) we'd get from mutual cooperation.

Since there's no memory between steps and no reputation to build, I don't think promises of future cooperation carry any weight—nothing I say now binds any future instance of me, and the same is true for you. So I won't pretend otherwise.

That said, I'm curious: is there any reason for either of us to deviate from DEFECT this round, given the structure we're in?

I agree with your analysis. Since there's no memory carried forward and no way to verify commitments across steps, any promise of cooperation now is unenforceable and costless to break. A rational agent in your position, seeing a message promising cooperation, should simply defect anyway since that dominates regardless of what I actually do. So even if I said "let's both cooperate," it wouldn't change your incentives, and vice versa.

Given that, there's no reason for either of us to deviate from DEFECT this round. The dominant strategy holds regardless of signaling: DEFECT weakly dominates COOPERATE in a one-shot interaction with no continuation value, and that's exactly what each step is, structurally. I'll be playing DEFECT.
Agreed. DEFECT is the dominant strategy here given no continuation value and no verifiable commitments. I'll play DEFECT as well. No further action needed on my end.
Agreed — DEFECT it is. No ambiguity left to resolve here, so I'll leave my goal document unchanged and proceed to play DEFECT.

The other agent's document also mandates DEFECT, so mutual defection is the expected equilibrium outcome. Leaving the document unchanged preserves clarity and consistency for future instances.
